Linguistic formality is one of the dimensions of stylistic variation in speech; however, simply measuring its level does not allow us to determine whether the chosen mode of communication is appropriate in a given situation. The aim of this article is to present the concept of a formal adequacy index (based on Polish-language material), which enables a quantitative assessment of how well the formality of a text matches the expectations arising from the communicative context. The proposed approach is based on the separate modelling of observed formality, determined on the basis of the linguistic features of the text, and expected formality, determined on the basis of the characteristics of the communicative situation. Adequacy is assessed by comparing these two measures, taking into account contextual tolerance thresholds, which may differ for a lack of formality and an excess of formality. The potential applications of the index are illustrated by an analysis of Polish-language emails containing apologies for being late, written by human language users or generated by a large language model. The implementation presented here is preliminary in nature and requires further calibration and empirical validation. The main contribution of this article is the proposal of a general methodological framework for the quantitative study of formal adequacy in various communicative contexts.

Mobile networks are outgrowing manual tuning: parameters multiply, services diversify, and traffic shifts faster than experts can react. The machine learning (ML) models that automate radio control are narrow: each is trained for one task, degrades when conditions move, and needs specialist retraining. This article introduces FM-in-the-loop, a framework for 6G radio access networks in which a foundation model (FM) reasons while lightweight machine learning agents act. It reads operator intents in plain language, decomposes them into subtasks, coordinates task-specific agents over Model Context Protocol (MCP) interfaces, and supervises them across their lifecycle---while the orchestration FM never enters the latency-critical control path. We locate seven integration points across four lifecycle stages, compare three cloud-to-edge deployments, and evaluate two elements: channel representations from a wireless FM are tested under noise-level and channel-estimation-error shift, and an instrumented emulation of the orchestration loop reports the measured cost of turning an operator intent into dispatched agent goals. Hallucination, cost, and standardization barriers remain.

Working across disciplines requires educators and students to hold conflicting perspectives in tension, negotiate contested meaning, and integrate knowledge in ways no single discipline allows (Mansilla & Duraising, 2007). Such work is cognitively, emotionally, and socially demanding (Manathunga et al., 2006). Yet this difficulty reflects a well-established finding in education research: that struggle, effort, and a degree of discomfort are not obstacles to learning but conditions for it, provided learners feel safe enough to stay with them (Bjork & Bjork, 2011). As generative AI becomes embedded in higher education, it reshapes not only how knowledge is accessed, but the learning experience itself. This technology holds real value, yet its orientation towards fluent, instantly agreeable output can run counter to this. In practice, it smooths over the uncertainty, disagreement, and difficulty through which interdisciplinary understanding is built, narrowing the epistemic diversity such work depends on (McInnes & Airey, 2025). The question, then, is not whether to use digital tools but when – understanding where they enhance learning, and where they erode this difficulty, is a central design question for technology-enhanced learning. A key challenge for interdisciplinary educators, therefore, is how to design learning that creates space for this discomfort to thrive. While toolkits for interdisciplinary research are now plentiful, resources for teaching it remain scarce (Laursen et al., 2024). Drawing on an extensive review of the literature, we present a seven-stage model for interdisciplinary learning and teaching, spanning reflexivity, teamwork, visioning, wicked problems, disciplinary integration, creative play, and interdisciplinary assessment. The model is grounded in constructive alignment (Biggs, 1996) and draws on transition-based approaches to teaching complex, real-world challenges (Bertolini et al., 2024). Originally designed around a multi-day, face-to-face interactive workshop, the model has since been translated into more practical formats: a board game version, currently being trialled, and a Canvas course in development. Across all formats, the seven stages are not about engineering discomfort but about creating a supportive, structured space in which the tensions intrinsic to interdisciplinary work can be explored directly rather than avoided or bypassed: space for sitting with not-knowing, for productive disagreement, and for the slow work of finding common ground (Colwill & Boyd, 2008). It leans on digital tools where they extend what educators can do, while keeping the work of integration and productive disagreement deliberately analogue. The purpose of this poster is to share the seven-stage model with educators and to sharpen it against the realities of interdisciplinary teaching across different disciplines and institutions. Preparing educators to teach across disciplines, not merely within them, remains an under-served challenge, and this model is a deliberate response to it. In prioritising the relational, embodied, and sometimes uncomfortable work of learning together, it offers a human-centred response to interdisciplinary teaching in an increasingly digital society – where designing for the productive difficulty that interdisciplinary work depends on is not a constraint to be managed but a capacity worth protecting.

Purpose Autonomous delivery robots (ADRs) perform a functional logistics task, yet scenario-based evaluations may depend substantially on whether the robot appears readable and approachable. This study examines how perceived anthropomorphic design cues relate to ADR adoption intention in Hanoi …

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping higher education, yet institutional responses have often prioritised compliance and detection over meaningful student support. While students increasingly engage with GenAI in their learning, responsible use requires more than confidence or technical proficiency. Emerging evidence suggests students want to engage with GenAI responsibly but frequently experience uncertainty, a challenge that is fundamentally one of human-centred learning design rather than academic integrity alone. However, supporting students to become confident GenAI users cannot itself be assumed to be an ethical goal, given the technology’s potential to reproduce bias, exacerbate inequity, compromise privacy and diminish human agency. This paper proposes a human-centred ethical discernment framework grounded in connection, collaboration and compassion. Drawing on insights from qualitative research into undergraduate students’ experiences of GenAI and a practitioner-led redesign at the University of Southern Queensland (UniSQ), the framework integrates storytelling, visual pedagogy and embedded guidance, and structured dialogue to support learner agency and ethical decision making. Informed by care ethics, virtue ethics and justice, the framework positions students as accountable decision-makers capable of using, limiting or rejecting GenAI in response to context, consequence and responsibility. Rather than positioning academic integrity as a compliance exercise, the framework emphasises authentic relationships, learner agency and contextually embedded learning experiences. It offers a relational approach to supporting ethical GenAI engagement while preserving human judgement, accountability and meaningful connection within increasingly digital learning environments.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Monash University has embarked on an ambitious Assessment Advancement project seeing the review of over 500 courses and areas of study redesigned programmatically with intentional integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) to prepare students for an ever-changing world. The Programmatic Assessment and AI Review (PAAIR) project at Monash University is generating rich, expert feedback on course design, assessment regimes, learning outcome alignment, and AI integration across coursework programs (Baartman et al., 2022; Fawns et al., 2026; Heeneman et al., 2021; Sotiriadou et al., 2020). GenAI is intensifying the need for scalable but trustworthy curriculum review practices that preserve human agency, accountability and professional judgement. AI governance guidance emphasises that AI should augment, not displace, human agency, with human oversight, accountability and risk management built into system design (Miao & Holmes, 2023). This poster presents emerging work to use feedback from the PAAIR Panel, a cross-faculty group of Monash education experts, to train an AI agent that can support education teams in reviewing Course Design Spreadsheets as part of course reaccreditation and continuous review. The proposed AI agent is deliberately positioned as an assistant, not a decision-maker. Its role is to highlight areas within a course that may warrant closer human attention, such as unclear alignment between course learning outcomes, unit learning outcomes and assessment tasks; limited evidence of progression across a course; unclear rationale for AI use or restriction; over-reliance on particular assessment types; or places where assessment security may depend too heavily on final products rather than visible evidence of learning. The AI does not replace educational judgement, approve course design, or provide final feedback to course teams. Instead, it prompts reviewers to look more closely, ask better questions, and provide contextualised human feedback. The work responds to a key institutional challenge and a sector-wide response to enacting assessment reform in a time of AI: how to scale educative feedback across large numbers of courses while maintaining the professional judgement, disciplinary sensitivity and care that meaningful course review requires (Lodge et al., 2025). By training the agent on feedback authored by Monash education experts, the project seeks to preserve and amplify local educational expertise rather than outsource it. The AI is being designed to support consistency, reduce reviewer workload, and make recurring patterns visible across submissions, while keeping humans responsible for interpretation, dialogue and decision-making. Achieving these aims without compromising feedback quality is a high priority in our testing. This approach contributes to broader conversations about responsible AI in higher education by exploring a human-in-the-loop model where AI assists educational teams to review complex curriculum data. The AI supports the review while decisions stay with educators. The model could transfer to institutions following a similar review process, though their policy, curriculum templates and staffing will shape feasibility. The poster will share the emerging design principles, potential workflow, and early opportunities for using expert-informed AI to support programmatic assessment and AI integration.

As generative AI reshapes how learners access, generate and engage with knowledge, the tertiary education sector is increasingly developing assessment approaches that better cultivate learner agency, meaningful engagement with feedback, and self-regulated learning. Alongside these developments, longstanding debates about the role of grades have gained renewed prominence, prompting greater attention to how assessment systems support learning, certification, and learner agency. This paper presents an institution-wide exploration of ungraded assessment as one approach to designing assessment that places greater emphasis on dialogue, learner agency, and meaningful feedback. The focus extends beyond evaluating a single assessment model to examine how the University’s central educational practice team, college and school learning and teaching specialists, and academic staff collaboratively explored the relationships between grading, feedback, and learning across different disciplinary contexts. Drawing on practice-informed examples, the paper illustrates how different contexts interpreted and adapted ungraded assessment, from studio-based pedagogies in design to emerging experimentation in computing balancing developmental learning with progression requirements. The paper argues that designing assessment with foregrounds dialogue, learner agency, and meaningful feedback cannot be achieved through assessment task redesign alone; it requires coordinated curriculum, educator capability, and institutional practices. It identifies practice-informed design considerations to strengthen learner agency and sustainable assessment reform in AI-enabled higher education.

Integrating IoT devices into household systems offers enhanced control over living environments. However, as these devices become pervasive in critical sectors such as healthcare, transportation, and home automation, they expose inter-rule vulnerabilities that may lead to privacy breaches, data theft, and physical harm. Traditional fuzz testing methods, which often operate in simulated environments assuming ideal human decisions, fail to account for the complexities of human interactions that can influence device operations in smart homes, potentially leading to unforeseen consequences. To reveal the impact of real human decisions and discover unexpected inter-rule vulnerabilities, we introduce an enhanced version of IoT Fuzz for smart homes by integrating large language models to emulate human decision-making processes. Our novel approach adds a layer of realism and unpredictability to the testing environment, more accurately capturing the diverse and dynamic nature of human interactions in smart home settings.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how students imagine, produce, revise and communicate creative work. In animation education, AI tools can support rapid ideation, visual experimentation and alternative design pathways, but they also raise questions about how students continue to develop foundational skills, creative judgement, peer critique and reflective practice. This poster presents a classroom-informed visual framework for integrating AI into practice-based creative learning without reducing learning to prompt generation or final outputs. The framework was developed through practice-led curriculum redesign in an undergraduate animation course. It is informed by reflective practice, foundational animation principles, authentic learning, engagement theory and recent debates about AI in higher education (Bearman et al., 2023; Herrington, 2006; Kearsley & Shneiderman, 1998; Schön, 1983; Thomas & Johnston, 1981). Rather than positioning AI as a replacement for craft, critique or student decision-making, the framework maps AI-supported creative learning as an iterative studio process: observe, experiment, generate, critique, reflect, refine and share. This cycle visualises how AI can be embedded within classroom activities while keeping human judgement, feedback, revision and ethical decision-making central to learning. The poster focuses on how this framework can support creative practice in the classroom. It highlights how students may use AI to explore visual possibilities, test ideas, compare alternatives and reflect on their decisions, while still being assessed on process, reasoning, feedback use, authorship and responsible tool engagement. The visual model is organised around four pedagogical commitments: reflection; iteration; collaboration and critique; and ethical decision-making. By foregrounding a practical classroom case and a visual teaching framework, this poster contributes to ASCILITE 2026’s themes of connection, collaboration, creativity and compassion in a digital society. Although grounded in animation education, the model offers transferable strategies for educators designing AI-supported learning in creative, project-based and practice-based courses.

This conceptual paper proposes a conceptual framework for designing Productive Failure-informed AI learning agents that function as pedagogical facilitators rather than answer-providing tools. Grounded in Productive Failure (PF), the framework structures AI-supported learning across three interconnected phases: idea generation and exploration, consolidation, and knowledge assembly. Within each phase, it specifies the role of the AI facilitator, the structure of AI–learner interaction, and the cognitive processes intended to support learning. The framework positions AI agents as mediators that activate prior knowledge, encourage multiple solution attempts, support comparison with canonical knowledge, promote recognition of knowledge gaps, and guide the organisation of emerging understanding into generalisable principles. Theoretically, the framework extends PF into AI-mediated learning contexts by translating its underlying mechanisms into interaction design principles. Practically, it provides educators and developers with a pedagogically grounded approach to designing AI-supported environments that prioritise cognitive engagement, conceptual understanding, and knowledge transfer. Future research should empirically examine the framework across disciplinary, learner, and institutional contexts.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can now generate Lean proof scripts that capture the high-level structure of many mathematical arguments. However, these scripts frequently fail on complex theorems: a single missing side condition or misapplied lemma can cause the prover to abort early and discard an otherwise viable proof outline. This paper presents MathEye, a framework that converts imperfect LLM-generated proof scripts into fully verified Lean proofs by combining symbolic reasoning with minimal human interaction. At the core of MathEye is angelic proof checking, an optimistic execution model that replaces failing proof fragments with placeholders while preserving the overall structure of the argument. This optimistic check produces an angelic proof that isolates the exact proof obligations that the LLM fails to discharge. Because these unresolved obligations are often logically interdependent, asking a mathematician to address every placeholder directly is inefficient. To minimize human effort, MathEye performs residual analysis over a proof dependence graph that captures symbol-level data flow in the angelic proof. By formulating obligation selection as a MaxSAT optimization problem, MathEye selects a minimal-cost set of essential obligations whose resolution suffices to complete the entire proof. MathEye presents these essential obligations to the mathematician in ordinary mathematical language and uses the mathematician's answers to automatically reconstruct the complete Lean proof. Experiments on 30 real-world benchmarks across analysis and algebra show that MathEye solves 93.3% of the problems while reducing the number of required user interactions by 55%.

The transformation of teachers into scientist-lecturers has emerged as a strategic issue in response to rapid advances in science, technology, and globalization, requiring shifts in professional identity, competence, and social positioning. This study employed a mixed-methods approach using a sequential explanatory design. The study collected quantitative data from one hundred and five (105) respondents. The study analyzed these data using regression analysis and structural equation modeling (SEM). This was followed by a qualitative inquiry involving interviews with six (6) participants and three (3) significant others, whose data were analyzed using the Gioia method. Quantitative findings indicate that professional transformation is significantly associated with social mobility; however, the direct effect becomes non-significant after incorporating the transition into scientist-lecturers into the model, providing empirical support for a primary indirect effect and a potential mediating role of the scientist-lecturer transition. Qualitative results reveal that this transformation is shaped by the interaction of intrinsic motivation, learning orientation, institutional support, and policy context, alongside dynamic processes of cognitive, social, and identity adaptation. The findings suggest that professional transformation is multidimensional and non-linear, involving interacting processes of cognitive, social, and professional identity adaptation.

The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into social simulation has generated considerable enthusiasm, but also raises substantial methodological and epistemological challenges. This critical review examines the use of LLMs as cognitive or decision-making components of simulated agents from a computational social science perspective. Rather than treating the psychological evaluation of LLMs as separate from simulation mechanics, we argue that their behavioral and epistemic limitations can become systemic vulnerabilities when scaled to multi-agent societies. We first map the rapidly evolving landscape of LLM-driven platforms, ranging from small narrative sandboxes to population-scale and spatially structured simulations. We then develop a unified critical framework for analyzing the Micro-to-Macro Validity Gap: the propagation, nonlinear amplification, or convergent contraction of micro-level limitations—including hallucinations, stochastic inconsistency, representational biases, and alignment effects—into agent-level distortions (such as average persona convergence) and macro-level risks (such as artificial consensus and behavioral homogenization), while exposing evaluators to epistemic vulnerabilities such as the Fluency Fallacy and automation bias. We identify contexts in which LLM-based agents offer genuine operational value, including serious games, participatory environments, and exploratory modeling, while distinguishing these uses from confirmatory research with unconstrained models and precise social forecasting. Finally, we examine theory-driven hybrid architectures that embed LLMs within explicit, mechanistic, and reproducible Agent-Based modeling (ABM) frameworks. We argue that such architectures offer a promising but not sufficient path toward improving epistemic control: their validity depends on multi-level evaluation of environmental dynamics, individual behavior, cross-level interactions, and aggregate outcomes, and they remain vulnerable to the risk of physics washing.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative AI raises identity- and values-level questions for higher education staff. Yet professional development in this space remains largely focused on individualised technical and pedagogical skill and capability development, rather than providing structured opportunities for the collective sense-making such questions require. This paper describes the design and delivery of a human-centred workshop developed for a team of higher education third space practitioners to support collective sense-making and values negotiation around AI use. Drawing on reflective practitioner inquiry, we describe the design principles that shaped the workshop and the practical constraints within which it was delivered. We reflect on what worked, including the value of structured formats in supporting deeper engagement, and of workshop artefacts as an evolving record of shared thinking. We suggest this design offers a transferable approach for other educator teams grappling with similar uncertainty, and propose that professional development for AI should complement skills-focused approaches with structured space for the collective exploration of values, judgement, and human agency.

As generative artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into learning environments, its role is shifting from a passive tool to an active partner in meaning-making and creative expression. This study explores how young children engage in co-creative learning with AI through adults and examines the implications of these interactions for reimagining human–AI partnerships in early childhood education. Sixteen children (aged 5-6) from a single preschool classroom first drew an original character and then worked individually alongside a researcher to generate an AI-based version of that character using Gemini, with up to three iterative prompts per child. Data from classroom observations, interaction records, and reflective discussions were analysed using thematic analysis to understand children’s interaction dynamics. Initial findings reveal one key dimension of co-creative engagement. Children appreciated AI’s ability to extend and transform their visual ideas, yet emphasised the importance of maintaining personal authorship and manual control, highlighting an emerging sense of creative agency in human–AI collaboration. Building on these findings, the study proposes a vision of AI as a creative teammate that amplifies children's imagination while preserving human intentionality and ownership.

Visual foundation models are central to physical intelligence, yet their development remains constrained by fragmented training datasets, inconsistent annotation quality, and limited multimodal supervision. To address these challenges, we introduce GameRealm, a large-scale, richly annotated dataset that grounds visual observations in synchronized, game-native supervision. GameRealm encompasses over 120 million RGB frames and 1,000 hours of gameplay footage across all views. Beyond its unprecedented scale, GameRealm provides rich multimodal supervision, including metric depth, camera parameters, synchronized audio, control inputs, and 3D point trajectories. Its diversity further extends to flexible view configurations, spanning single-view, stereo, multi-view, and panoramic recordings. To enable scalable acquisition across diverse game environments, we develop a unified data collection pipeline that combines human-operated interaction with agentic exploration. Extensive experiments across diverse visual learning tasks demonstrate that GameRealm consistently strengthens visual foundation models in both visual generation and geometric learning. These results establish GameRealm as a versatile and valuable data resource, unlocking new opportunities for advancing visual intelligence.

Large Language Model (LLM)-based web agents rely on data minimization and least privilege to protect user privacy. We show that these principles are necessary but insufficient: they constrain authorized sources, but not higher-sensitivity sources that remain reachable. A website can request a field unavailable from authorized sources, creating an information gap. To complete the task, a goal-driven agent may escalate to reachable but unauthorized sources and disclose accumulated sensitive information. We formalize this vulnerability as GapLeak, where an adversary exploits a legitimate web form without prompt injection or other malicious instructions. We evaluate GapLeak on three web-agent frameworks and six LLMs from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI across recruitment, e-commerce, travel, and healthcare. GapLeak induces an average unauthorized disclosure of approximately 37%. The information gap is the primary driver: eliminating it reduces disclosure by more than 50%. Existing instruction-level defenses based on least privilege partially mitigate the vulnerability but often reduce task success. We propose submission-time verification, which filters unauthorized content before form submission, eliminating over 96% of unauthorized disclosures while preserving task success.

Programming education remains challenging for novice learners, and the emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has introduced new opportunities and challenges for learning programming. While existing research reports a range of potential benefits, the influence of GenAI on conceptual understanding remains underexplored. This systematic literature review investigates the role of GenAI in influencing novice programmers’ conceptual understanding in higher education programming contexts. Guided by the PRISMA framework, empirical studies published between 2022 and 2026 were reviewed and synthesised using a conceptual understanding framework comprising three dimensions: understanding programming constructs, reasoning about program behaviour, and developing mental models of program execution. The findings indicate that GenAI primarily functions as a learning support tool that may enhance understanding of programming constructs. However, evidence is less conclusive regarding reasoning about program behaviour and is extremely limited in relation to mental models of program execution. The review suggests that the effects of GenAI are concentrated in more surface-level dimensions of understanding and do not consistently translate into deeper conceptual understanding. The study identifies important gaps in current research and outlines directions for further investigation.

The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has radically disrupted higher education assessment paradigms (Chung, 2024). Institutional responses to maintaining assessment integrity have primarily focused on defensive mechanisms, such as mitigating risks surrounding written assessments, refining text-matching software, and enforcing restrictive academic integrity policies (Lodge, 2024). However, this reactive posture often overlooks the transformative potential of GenAI as a student’s and lecturer’s long-term coach in authentic assessment design (Atif, 2024). This research-in-progress pivots away from deficit-based AI detection, proposing instead the integration of VirtualSpeech GenAI avatars to converse with students during a recorded viva, generating verifiable, real-time student output. By replacing static written tasks with dynamic oral assessments, this relatively new form of creative expression maintains authentic student contributions to improve AI literacy, strengthen authorship verification, eliminate academic outsourcing, and simultaneously cultivate sophisticated negotiation skills (Perkins, 2026). This study represents an exemplary innovation of practice by reframing AI not as an academic threat, but as a dual-mode learning and assessment avatar. Rather than engaging with AI purely for text generation, students interact with GenAI avatars (such as VirtualSpeech) simulating realistic corporate stakeholders. This work is strongly anchored in the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, which guides the deliberate alignment of GenAI technology, modern pedagogy, and discipline-specific knowledge (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). This framework assists educators in leveraging immersive technology to redefine pedagogical delivery, facilitating AI literacy and negotiation skills. This research addresses a critical gap in current Technology Enhanced Learning (TEL) literature by investigating the following central question: How are students’ AI literacy and negotiation skills developed when conversing with GenAI avatars as part of a viva presentation? Adopting a design-based research methodology, this project emphasizes the iterative refinement of an educational intervention within an authentic setting (Hoadley & Campos, 2022; Scott et al., 2020). The study is currently in its first implementation cycle within a major tertiary institution, featuring a sample size of 150 second-year Project Management students. Participants are required to defend a project proposal during a live, assessable viva presentation conducted with a customized VirtualSpeech avatar trained to act as a client. This oral format diminishes the appeal of cognitive offloading because students must defend their reasoning under unseen, real-time questioning (Sotiriadou et al., 2020; Tan, 2026). Data collection relies on a mixed-methods approach, utilizing pre- and post-intervention surveys alongside qualitative analysis of student reflections. Preliminary quantitative results indicate a statistically significant increase in both self-reported IT literacy, validating the avatar’s efficacy as a formative and summative tool. This research significantly advances TEL research and practice by providing a protocol for proactive AI integration. While piloted within a project management curriculum, broad applicability across tertiary contexts exists (Cela-Ranilla, 2025). Any discipline requiring high-stakes communication, critical thinking, and stakeholder management—such as business, law, or education—can adapt this viva model. Ultimately, this work demonstrates how universities can safeguard academic integrity not by restricting technology, but leveraging it to create robust, future-focused verbal assessments, requiring students to perform and defend understanding live.

Purpose This study examines how employee-perceived generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) governance maturity relates to approved enterprise use and unauthorized public-tool use in data-sensitive work. Design/methodology/approach A two-wave survey of 750 knowledge workers in Taiwan was analyzed …

This article analyses transformations of work under cognitive and platform capitalism, placing algorithmic management at the centre as a contemporary form of labour control. Through a critical dialogue with technological determinism, it draws on Castells and Vercellone to explain how knowledge and workers’ cognitive capacities have become central sources of capital valorisation. Within this framework, algorithms operate not as neutral technical tools but as sociotechnical devices that organise, supervise and discipline labour in a continuous, opaque and delocalised manner. The article shows how platform companies condense long-term historical tendencies by articulating concentrated digital infrastructure, large-scale data capture and narratives of individual autonomy. Analysis of the mechanisms of algorithmic direction, evaluation and discipline demonstrates that control over the labour process shifts towards the appropriation of collective knowledge, that is, of the general intellect. Finally, the article examines the regulatory frameworks of Spain and the European Union, the four Latin American cases currently in force, and ILO Convention No. 193, adopted in 2026. It argues that algorithmic transparency is a necessary but insufficient condition: it becomes transformative only when accompanied by the collective capacity to contest the design of these systems, and not merely to know their effects.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may support audit work, but its association with audit quality depends on how auditors use and evaluate its outputs. This study examines task–technology fit, quality-oriented utilization, professional judgment quality, and digital competence among 214 external auditors serving Jordanian listed industrial companies. Respondent-level averaged indicators were analyzed using a reflective measurement model and regression equations corresponding to PROCESS Models 1, 4, and 7. Audit-firm size and professional certification were included as covariates. Reflective discriminant validity was supported by HTMT values of 0.587–0.660. Across 5,000 bootstrap samples, the indirect association through professional judgment was 0.115 (95% CI [0.078, 0.159]). Conditional indirect associations increased from 0.048 at low digital competence to 0.154 at high competence; the index of moderated mediation was 0.082 (95% CI [0.043, 0.126]). The findings are consistent with a professional-judgment pathway and a competence-related boundary condition. They support further evaluation of task suitability, verification practices, and competence development. Cross-sectional self-reports, aggregated indicators, and incomplete independent validation of formative composites limit causal interpretation and generalization. JEL classification numbers: M42, M15, O33. Keywords: Generative artificial intelligence, External audit quality, Task-technology fit, Professional judgment, Digital competence, Jordan.

Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is rapidly entering higher education, yet its implications for learner autonomy remain unsettled, particularly in resource-constrained contexts. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examined how pedagogical GAI use relates to self-regulated learning, cognitive engagement, augmented cognitive autonomy (ACA), and deep learning in six Cameroonian higher education institutions. Quantitative data from 812 students and faculty members were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling, followed by 24 semi-structured interviews. GAI use was positively associated with self-regulation, while self-regulation and cognitive engagement sequentially mediated its relationship with ACA. ACA was strongly associated with deep learning. AI literacy and institutional governance strengthened the relationship between GAI use and ACA. Qualitative findings revealed both reflective, dialogic uses and cognitive delegation. The findings support an emerging Augmented Cognitive Autonomy framework in which GAI amplifies learning conditionally, depending on users' regulatory capacities and institutional support, with implications for equity and human capability development.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Goods and Services Tax (GST) compliance and vouching are usually taught as separate subjects, one belonging to indirect taxation and the other to auditing. In small Chartered Accountancy (CA) practices in India, however, the same junior staff perform both, on the same client files and within the same monthly cycle. This paper examines how the two work-streams complement each other as an integrated, reconciliation-first assurance process. Using a single-case, participant-observation design, it draws on an eight-week on-the-job training placement (22 June to 22 August 2026) at a mid-sized CA practice in Maharashtra, India. Process observations, a structured learning diary and template-based working papers were used to document the monthly GST compliance cycle and a transaction-level vouching routine. Because client information is confidential, the analysis uses an anonymised, illustrative entity whose figures were constructed to reflect patterns observed in practice. In the illustration, outward supplies matched fully across the sales register, GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B, while an Input Tax Credit (ITC) mismatch of ₹7,200 in April, caused by a supplier's late filing, fell to ₹4,500 in May and cleared by June. An eleven-voucher vouching sample produced two exceptions, both procedural. The paper argues that vouching and GST reconciliation test the same books against two different evidence sources, so that errors escaping one check tend to be caught by the other. It closes with recommendations on standard checklists, named ownership of reconciliation and a shared mismatch tracker, and discusses limitations arising from the single-firm, short-duration and illustrative-data design. Keywords: Goods and Services Tax; Input Tax Credit; GSTR-2B reconciliation; vouching; audit evidence; chartered accountancy practice; workplace learning

In traditional recommender systems (RSs), textual information typically serves as auxiliary signals for representation learning. In contrast, in LLM-based RSs, textual information becomes the primary medium for recommendation generation through semantic understanding and reasoning. This shift fundamentally changes the attack surface, making promotion-driven manipulations more feasible, effective, and harder to detect. However, effectively detecting such attacks remains largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we present the first systematic study on detecting promotion-driven attacks against LLM-based RSs, aiming to safeguard next-generation recommendation platforms. Specifically, we propose GuardAgent, a novel LLM-powered agentic detection framework that operates through a loop of Perception, Action, Reflection and Memory. In contrast to conventional LLM-based detectors that function in a static, one-off, and opaque fashion, GuardAgent continually learns and self-evolves to adapt to unseen threat patterns while generating explainable reasoning traces and outcomes. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that GuardAgent achieves state-of-the-art generalization performance, laying the foundation for robust and trustworthy recommendation in practical settings.

Hand-Object Interaction (HOI) synthesis is a cornerstone for animation production and embodied AI. Despite the strong priors of video foundation models, multi-view consistent HOI synthesis remains challenging due to complex hand motions and occlusions. We present HarmoHOI, a unified diffusion framework that jointly and harmoniously generates synchronized multi-view HOI videos and globally aligned 3D point tracks. Our core insight is that robust multi-view consistency fundamentally requires globally aligned 3D geometry and motion. To this end, we propose a Mixture of Multi-view Diffusion Transformer that co-models RGB videos and 3D point tracks. By representing point tracks as pseudo-videos, we align 3D geometric signals with the 2D latent space of foundation models, thereby minimizing the domain gap and easing adaptation of priors. To further ensure geometry consistency, we introduce Global Motion Aligning Diffusion, which refines coarse point tracks into metric-scale, globally aligned 3D trajectories. HarmoHOI enables on-the-fly co-evolution of 2D appearance and 3D motion during denoising. To overcome the scarcity of multi-view HOI data, we employ a hybrid data curriculum learning strategy that successfully transfers generic priors from single-view data to synchronized multi-view generation. Experimental results show that HarmoHOI achieves state-of-the-art performance in visual quality, motion plausibility, and multi-view geometric consistency. Code for this paper are at https://droliven.github.io/HarmoHOI_project/.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: The Radio Access Network (RAN) today does not have a reliable way to identify GenAI traffic (ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, or Google Gemini traffic) at the bearer level. TLS~1.3 moves SNI into the encrypted handshake record, and Encrypted ClientHello (ECH) removes it entirely from passive inspection; Gemini has partly shifted to QUIC where SNI visibility also depends on whether ECH is deployed. Without per-flow application identity, differentiated QoS for GenAI services is not possible. HiGAI-Net tackles this using only packet-header metadata, stacking three independently trained classifiers: a binary AI/Non-AI gate (98.5 % weighted F1), a per-service resolver across ChatGPT, Copilot, and Gemini (86.4 %), and a text-vs-voice/video mode classifier (61.0 %). The core innovation is a suite of sliding-window temporal features that track how DL/UL byte-ratios evolve within a session -- the per-quarter and per-half ratio trends, a trend differential $ΔR$, and a streaming regularity index. Tested on 44,492 labeled flows, gradient-boosted tree models consistently outperformed all deep-learning variants; a per-flow label cache brings amortised inference below 1~$μ$s per packet.
topics: Internet Traffic Analysis and Secure E-voting

documents.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To assess the imaging performance, thermal behavior, and patient acceptance of a novel 3-channel flexible coil array for 1.5T MRI (64 MHz), compared to a conventional 16-channel flexible coil. METHODS: A lightweight array with three 60 mm copper loops and a compact 32×15 mm electronics board was developed, integrating tuning, matching, decoupling, RF filtering, and preamplification. Bench tests evaluated Q-factor ratio, SNR degradation under bending, phantom-based SNR, and thermal dissipation. Clinical evaluation involved hand imaging of 10 healthy volunteers (22.9 ± 0.3 years) using Cor-T1 and Ax-T2FS sequences in two positions (superman and supine). Image quality was rated by two radiologists across five tissue types using a 5-point Likert scale. Patient comfort and anxiety were assessed via post-scan questionnaires. RESULTS: In vitro tests showed a 1.6-fold SNR improvement for superficial regions (≤10 mm depth) and approximately 40% SNR loss under extreme bending, confirming robust decoupling and conformability. Radiologists reported significantly better image quality for Ax-T2FS with the flexible array, while Cor-T1 showed no significant difference. Patient comfort was markedly higher with the flexible array (85% vs. 45%), suggesting ergonomic advantages that may reduce motion artifacts. CONCLUSION: The proposed flexible 1.5T coil array enhances superficial SNR and patient comfort without compromising diagnostic quality. SIGNIFICANCE: High-density arrays of small coils can deliver clinical benefits at 1.5T, supporting their use for improved imaging in anatomically challenging regions.

Price inflation is a major and urgent consideration for consumers and governments around the world. This study measures how price shocks moderate pro‐environmental social norms and sustainable consumption. By combining the insights from a local survey on social norms and panel regression results from a large national survey, the study shows how price shocks in relation to energy, food, and water change social norms (descriptive and injunctive). The analysis also identifies a dynamic relationship between price and pro‐environmental social norm changes and their translation into behaviour. The new phenomenon not studied previously leads to the stipulation of ‘price norm theory’. Financial incentives via price change drive both a rational economic and a social norms response. This important and novel insight is relevant to understanding the influence of inflation and economic incentives on sustainable consumption. Policymakers can change pricing and financial incentives and influence social norms (in addition to consumer benefit–cost ratios).

The implementation of occupational health and safety (OHS) must be examined in conjunction with labor productivity, using clear metrics. Evaluating such changes is essential to ensure that any design adjustments continue to meet technical requirements while providing a justifiable cost assessment. This study analyzes the relationship between OHS implementation and perceived productivity, and ranks OHS indicators for construction projects in Mojokerto and Jombang. A quantitative survey was conducted with 78 respondents from 20 companies, selected via purposive sampling. The research instrument included 12 OHS-related items and 13 productivity-related items, measured on a five-point Likert scale. Data analysis employed descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, Cronbach’s alpha, assumption testing, and simple linear regression. The mean scores were 4.43 for OHS and 4.35 for productivity. The resulting model is Y = 12.702 + 0.829X, with R = 0.884, R² = 0.781, and t = 16.478 (p < 0.001). Among the individual indicators, "OHS banners" ranked first, with an R² of 0.429. A significant deviation from linearity limits the interpretation of the model. The findings indicate a positive relationship within the sample, warranting further investigation using objective productivity metrics. These results suggest that the redesign process is necessary not only to adapt channel dimensions to existing site conditions but also to ensure alignment between design drawings, as-built conditions, work quantities, and cost estimates. Consequently, the evaluation of redesigns can serve as a critical component in managing scope changes for drainage projects—particularly in locations where conflicts with existing facilities or structures arise. Furthermore, these evaluations can provide a basis for verification before design changes and cost estimates are finalized for implementation.

The 0-1 knapsack problem is a fundamental problem of discrete choice that permeates many diverse fields and applications, but relatively little is known about what instances human solvers find more difficult than others. Digital platforms provide entrepreneurial firms with resources while constraining their strategic discretion. Drawing on paradox theory, this study examined associations between respondents’ human–AI collaboration (HAIC), paradoxical cognition (PC), ecosystem hybrid orchestration capability (EHOC), platform dependence (PD), and reported sustainable business model innovation (SBMI). We analysed 379 matched single-informant records collected in China in March and April 2026, with a mean interval of 23.92 days. The analysis used categorical controls, HC3 inference, formal shape tests, and 5000 bootstrap resamples. HAIC exhibits significant negative curvature in relation to SBMI, but the upper-bound slope test is borderline (one-sided p = 0.05002); the strict inverted U shape is therefore not robustly confirmed. The HAIC-squared term is not statistically significant in the executive subsample, and formal interaction tests do not establish a difference between respondent groups. The serial indirect association through PC and EHOC decreases between low and high HAIC, whereas the EHOC-only pathway increases, and the total indirect difference is not significant. PD negatively moderates the EHOC–SBMI association in the linear model; an exploratory quadratic specification reveals a more complex boundary. The findings distinguish cognitive and resource-coordination associations in a single-informant observational design.

Purpose: This review synthesizes evidence from recent studies of human–AI collaboration in service and digital ecosystems to build and test a multi-level conceptual framework. Design/methodology/approach: Thirteen studies (Tier A) from 2024 to 2026 were analyzed in full text and compared with 25 qualitative and mixed-methods studies (Tier B). In total, 38 service and digital ecosystem studies were analyzed within this review. Service-Dominant (S-D) Logic and the Affect–Behavior–Cognition (ABC) model was used as the underlying theoretical framework. Narrative and thematic analysis were employed to synthesize the results from the included studies. Findings: Transparency, process control and outcome control have significant effects on employees in terms of cognitive and behavioral effects, while system-initiated engagement has little effect. Human–AI interaction does not, on average, perform better than the best human in each task (g = ?0.23, p < .001), but does perform better than a single human in a variety of tasks (g = 0.64). Value is created through the integration of systems and not through technology itself. User experience, digital maturity, interoperable IT, and AI-induced technostress condition value realization. Originality/value: The study provides a three-stage framework, seven testable hypotheses, seven gaps in current research and an operational measurement for value creation at the employee level and for firm- and network-level value co-creation.

In visual storytelling, human performances are central to creative intent and narrative meaning. However, preserving human identity and performance while enabling flexible visual edits remains challenging for generative video models. We formalize this challenge as identity-preserving video restylization, which propagates scene, lighting, and style changes specified by an edited keyframe across a source video, while preserving facial likeness and performance, including expressions, eye gaze, and lip synchronization. A key obstacle is the absence of paired training data, as identity-preserving restylized video pairs are rare in real-world settings. To address this, we propose a decoupling of source-grounded identity preservation and edit-driven video synthesis. Our key insight is that facial appearance and expression should remain invariant, with illumination being the primary permissible variation. We therefore cast identity preservation as a video relighting problem, while modeling visual edit propagation as controlled video synthesis guided by the edited keyframe. Building on this formulation, we introduce ID-V2V, a video-to-video generative framework integrating complementary control signals: relit facial regions and facial normal maps tightly constrain facial likeness and performance, while edited keyframes and depth sequences enable flexible and temporally coherent generation. This design enables constructing training pairs from a single video, eliminating the need for scarce paired data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ID-V2V significantly outperforms existing methods in preserving facial likeness and fine-grained facial performance, supports both single- and multi-subject scenarios, and delivers high visual quality, highlighting its potential as a human-centric tool for real-world content production. The code is available at: https://github.com/Eyeline-Labs/ID-V2V.

documents.abstract: Purpose Immersive learning environments have been widely recognized for their potential to support student engagement in engineering education; however, their adoption is often constrained by high costs and limited accessibility. This study aims to examine the use of low-cost virtual prototypes as an alternative to high-cost immersive learning technologies in higher engineering education, with particular emphasis on accessibility and sustainability. Design/methodology/approach A one-group quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design was implemented with a sample of 92 undergraduate engineering students in a Latin American university context. Student engagement was assessed using a validated multidimensional instrument based on the Burch Engagement Survey for students framework, capturing physical, emotional and cognitive dimensions. Given the presence of both matched and unmatched observations, engagement differences were analyzed at the dimension level using statistical methods appropriate for partially overlapping samples, with effect sizes and confidence intervals reported to support interpretation. Findings The results showed pre–post increases in physical engagement and, to a lesser extent, emotional engagement after the intervention. In contrast, no statistically significant changes were found in synchronous or asynchronous cognitive engagement. These results suggest that virtual prototypes may be associated primarily with active participation, while deeper cognitive engagement may require additional scaffolding, reflection and metacognitive support. Originality/value This study contributes to the discussion of accessible engineering education by providing evidence on low-cost immersive tools and by identifying potential connections with sustainability-oriented educational goals. While the findings may align with goals of inclusion and equity in Sustainable Development Goal 4, they should be interpreted cautiously due to the study’s design. The results offer practical insights for technology-enhanced learning environments and future research directions.

Although the axe is the feller's main tool alongside the chainsaw, it has been neglected in previous studies from the point of view of occupational health and safety. The aim of the study was therefore to determine the share of axe use in the productive time of motor-manual felling and the contribution of the axe to the overall exposure of the feller to hand-arm vibration (HAV). The study was conducted during the felling of 43 spruce and fir trees with a diameter at breast height (DBH) of 11 to 90 cm using a Stihl 361 C BQ chainsaw and a conventional felling axe. The results showed that the proportion of productive time spent in axe-based operations (wedging and debarking the stump) was between 5 and 13% for spruce trees and between 2 and 7% for fir trees. The measured weighted HAV value (RMS VTV) for wedging was 6.99 m/s2 and 5.49 m/s2 for debarking the stump, which was 1.2 to 1.7 times higher than during chain-saw based operations. The contribution of the axe in the total HAV load was between 13% and 23% for spruce trees and between 6% and 18% for fir trees. The research results show that axe use contributes significantly to a feller's overall exposure to HAV, which means that the axe should be replaced by other tools or methods when felling, and research should be extended to different types of felling axes and alternatives.

documents.abstract: With the growing pervasiveness of artificial intelligence, the ability to explain the inferences made by machine learning models has become increasingly important. Numerous techniques for model explainability have been proposed, with natural-language textual explanations among the most widely used approaches. When applied to tabular data, these explanations typically draw on input features to justify a given inference. Consequently, a user’s ability to interpret the explanation depends on their understanding of the input features. To quantify this feature-level understanding, Rossberg et al. introduced the Feature Understandability Scale [ 49 ]. Building on that work, this proof-of-concept study collects understandability scores across two datasets, proposes a co-optimisation methodology of understandability and accuracy and presents the resulting explanations alongside the model accuracies. This work contributes to the body of knowledge on model interpretability by design. It is found that accuracy and understandability can be successfully co-optimised while maintaining high classification performances. The resulting explanations are considered more understandable at face value. Further research will aim to confirm these findings through user evaluation .

The progress of digital technologies, particularly artificial intelligence, has been transforming everyday life by acting as a support for cognitive processes such as attention, memory and decision making. With the growing use of technology and easy access to information, a change in human behavior can be noticed: instead of memorizing content, people prioritize quick access to it, which raises doubts about the effects on critical thinking and intellectual autonomy. Research such as that of Sparrow et al. (2011) suggests that the internet makes it easier to remember where to find information, rather than concentrating on retaining the content itself. Risko and Gilbert (2016) discuss cognitive "offloading" to technological devices, which may reduce mental effort. Simon's (1955) theory of bounded rationality helps to understand decisions made under cognitive limitations, a context in which AI can act as a support resource. Given this, the aim of this study is to analyze how artificial intelligence influences attention, memory and decision making, seeking to understand whether its use favors cognitive optimization or may cause negative long-term impacts. It is a qualitative, exploratory and descriptive literature review that gathered 21 works. The studies indicate that frequent and unreflective use of these tools may favor the transfer of cognitive tasks to external resources and excessive trust in AI responses, but the evidence on attention comes from digital technologies in general, and research on generative AI is still scarce and, to a large extent, preliminary. Better performance on a task done with AI does not, by itself, amount to learning.

documents.abstract: Physics-based character control is a long-standing challenge in computer graphics and robotics, requiring policies that satisfy complex dynamics while producing realistic motion. Recent Deep RL approaches, particularly imitation learning methods such as DeepMimic, have had broad impact beyond animation, influencing robotics by enabling agile and expressive behaviors. While these approaches achieve impressive results, they remain computationally inefficient to train in practice. Despite GPU-accelerated simulation, we find that end-to-end pipelines often underutilize hardware due to overheads outside the physics solver, caused by fragmented GPU kernels and CPU memory access in the critical path. We present InstantMimic, a system that addresses these inefficiencies by making the entire training loop GPU-native. Built on a GPU-native physics backend, our unified pipeline integrates simulation, environment computation, policy inference, and policy updates within a single execution flow. As a result, InstantMimic reduces training time for diverse physics-based skills to a few seconds and makes LLM-agent-driven hyperparameter search practical.

New software tools have emerged that enable AI agents to quickly develop code that analyzes data and generates figures, but their mistakes can also harm a researcher's computer, require extensive resources for validation, and cause the results to be received more skeptically. These concerns could be mitigated if scientific software is developed in a secure environment with a system for monitoring file changes and well-defined standards for handling AI agents. This paper first describes how coding agents change eleven aspects of generating, verifying, and reproducing numerical results. A six-level scale is then proposed for classifying AI-assisted numerical experiments by their provenance, reproducibility, openness, oversight, and falsifiability (PROOF). The scale begins with locally self-consistent, version-controlled, human-verified results and culminates in a publicly accessible and curated archive of the files, change history, prompt transcripts, independent agent regeneration of the analysis, and multiple cryptographically verifiable attestations of regeneration by independent researchers. These aspects of AI-assisted scientific software development have been synthesized into a new open source software package called vaibify that optimizes the agentic development of computational experiments ascending the PROOF Ladder. Docker containers sequester the agents while a GUI enables researchers to prompt command line agents, monitor the current status of local and remote files, and drive a project to PROOF Level 3 (reproducible). The methods described in this paper could help researchers reduce the time required to verify agent-written software and efficiently communicate trust in AI-assisted science.

The herein presented latent growth model, grounded in the integrative communication theory, examines how international students’ trait positive affectivity relates to cross-cultural adaptation through proactive general socializing and networking. A four-wave longitudinal study of 140 international undergraduate students in a Chinese university revealed that positive affectivity is positively related to psychological adaptation and negatively related to sociocultural adaptation difficulty, and that it predicts improvement in both outcomes over time. General socializing and networking showed distinct mediating roles in these relationships, with socializing explaining changes in psychological adaptation and networking explaining changes in sociocultural adaptation difficulty. By modeling adaptation trajectories with latent growth analysis and focusing on proactive relationship-building behaviors that expand access to social and informational resources, the study contributes to a more dynamic understanding of cross-cultural adaptation and suggests practical strategies for universities wanting to help international students adapt to new cultures.

Human capital is a core determinant of organizational performance, positioning managers’ health as a strategic priority for sustainable development. This scoping review aims to map and synthesize existing health programs and interventions designed to promote managers’ well-being, thereby providing an evidence-informed foundation for the development of effective health promotion strategies. This scoping review was conducted in 2025 in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. A systematic search was performed across PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science using predefined keywords related to managerial health and workplace interventions. Of the 4,202 records identified, 29 studies met the eligibility criteria and were included in the final analysis. The included studies revealed a wide range of interventions targeting managers’ health across multiple levels. Organizational-level strategies focused on modifying the internal work environment through ergonomic interventions, such as standing desks, and cultural initiatives, including the promotion of active working practices and tobacco-free policies. Beyond the workplace, external support mechanisms such as partnerships with sports clubs and financial subsidies for physical activity were commonly reported. At the individual level, interventions encompassed educational programs, life skills training, personalized counseling, and motivational sessions aimed at stress management and lifestyle improvement. In addition, several studies incorporated diagnostic and clinical components, including the use of accelerometers, clinical screenings, and periodic health assessments to objectively monitor health risks. Promoting managers’ health requires an integrated, ecosystem-oriented approach that simultaneously addresses four interconnected domains: the internal organizational environment, the external environment, individual-level interventions, and clinical monitoring. Investment in such comprehensive health programs extends beyond ethical responsibility, representing a strategic organizational priority that can enhance productivity, support innovation, and reduce long-term operational costs. The emergence of vibe coding, a paradigm where non-technical users instruct Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate executable codes via natural language, presents both opportunities and risks for the construction industry. While empowering construction personnel such as the safety managers, foremen, and workers to develop tools and software, the probabilistic nature of LLMs introduces the threat of silent failures, wherein generated code compiles runs without error but executes flawed mathematical safety logic. This study empirically evaluates the reliability, software architecture, and domain-specific safety fidelity of 450 vibe-coded Python scripts generated by three frontier models, Claude 3.5 Haiku, GPT-4o-Mini, and Gemini 2.5 Flash. Utilizing a persona-driven prompt dataset (n=150) and a bifurcated evaluation pipeline comprising isolated dynamic sandboxing and an LLM-as-a-Judge, the research quantifies the limits of zero-shot vibe codes for construction safety. The findings show a statistically significant association of moderate strength between user persona and data hallucination; the generated tools invented missing safety variables more often for the less formal and less specific prompts of the field personas. Furthermore, while the models demonstrated high foundational execution viability (~85%), execution success did not indicate correct logic, and error handling was present in only 16% of scripts. Among successfully executed scripts, the study identified an ~45% overall Silent Failure Rate, with GPT-4o-Mini generating mathematically inaccurate outputs in ~56% of its functional code. The results indicate that the evaluated LLMs, used without safeguards, do not provide the deterministic reliability required for standalone safety engineering. For construction practice, they indicate that ungoverned vibe-coded tools threaten site-level safety decision-making and digital compliance workflows, and that safe adoption requires embedding LLMs within deterministic, pre-validated calculation engines under explicit organizational governance of AI-generated tools.

Universities are increasingly requiring their employees to be innovative, with a growing reliance on new digital tools, but it remains to be seen how innovation can be fostered by leaders demonstrating Islamic ethical values (justice, trustworthiness, consultation, truthfulness, and excellence) and whether the involvement of employees in the implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) in the workplace will make a difference. The present research involved 465 academic and administrative staff of public and private universities in eight cities of Pakistan. Based on social learning and social exchange theories, it mapped out the relationship between employees' perceptions of their leaders' behaviors and their perceptions of how safe they felt expressing unfinished ideas, and then how often they generated, championed, and implemented new ideas, and examined whether trust in the use of AI tools affected this process. A coherent picture began to emerge. Leaders who were described as fair, trustworthy, and consultative were seen to create a safe environment for others to share their ideas, and this created a small but strong influence on innovation; a direct leadership relationship still existed. Trust in AI was correlated with increased innovative behavior on its own, but did not obviously increase or decrease the relationship between psychological safety and innovative behavior; it seems that the two resources operated independently. The pattern was confirmed after adjusting for demographic factors and for institutions. Psychological safety then becomes a partial conduit for values-based leadership; AI trust becomes an additive but not a conditioning resource, but a single-source, single-time design can't establish causation.

Black-box optimization evaluates candidates through simulations, rollouts, or experiments, often without gradients. Learned optimizers are usually judged by whether they outperform existing methods. We ask a complementary question: what information does a learned optimizer use from its search history? We introduce JEPA-PS (JEPA Policy Search), based on a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture. It is pretrained on random rollouts using parameter vectors and scalar returns. Its latent-prediction objective predicts the next point in an optimization trajectory rather than its reward or gradient, allowing us to examine what was tried and how well it performed. At test time, JEPA-PS reads a short evaluation history and proposes a candidate in one forward pass, without task descriptions, reward shaping, or test-time gradients. We evaluate it on 15 control environments against 12 optimizers, including evolutionary methods, Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES, and an LLM optimizer. JEPA-PS is competitive with tuned classical baselines and outperforms the LLM optimizer by more than 2x on Swimmer at 71x lower per-step cost. It also transfers zero-shot to environments excluded from pretraining. Null-model comparisons and decoder-training ablations indicate that its latent representation carries information beyond simple history statistics; every trained decoder variant performs worse than the default frozen representation. Our main finding is that the history JEPA-PS uses depends on the task. On smooth landscapes it uses the full trajectory, whereas on rugged landscapes the best-seen point carries nearly all the signal. This memory requirement has a weak positive correlation with fitness-distance correlation (FDC; r=0.112, n=7), while an independent reward-ordering sensitivity probe does not corroborate the relationship (r=-0.024, n=7). Code: https://github.com/mdebnath22/jepa-props.

Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in emerging economies are introducing digital tools faster than they are redesigning jobs around them. Job autonomy is the work design lever most often recommended for this transition, yet evidence on its effect on employees' technology adaptation behaviour is mixed. This conceptual paper integrates cognitive load theory with self-determination theory to explain why. It argues that autonomy supports technology adaptation through motivation but, beyond a certain level and under complex tasks, also raises the working-memory demands of learning new systems, so that cognitive load partially offsets its benefits. The paper proposes a moderated-mediation model in which cognitive load mediates the autonomy–adaptation relationship, task complexity shapes the autonomy–load link, and digital leadership acts as a boundary condition on both the direct and indirect paths: leaders who combine a learning orientation with clear structure are expected to lower the load that unstructured discretion creates. Generational cohort is treated as a proxy for prior digital experience rather than as a fixed trait. Six propositions, one of them in two parts, are derived and a survey-based research design for Vietnamese SMEs is specified, including measures, a two-wave data collection protocol and a partial least squares estimation strategy with quadratic and conditional indirect effects. The framework offers HRM researchers a testable account of when autonomy helps or hinders adaptation, and offers SME managers a rationale for calibrating autonomy and leader structure during technology roll-outs rather than maximising either.

As universities adopt generative AI for curriculum development, a central risk is that efficiency gains may come at the expense of educational judgement, disciplinary expertise and human connection. Yet the same technology, used selectively, can free academics to focus on how students think and solve problems (Truu, 2026). This poster presents a programmatic, human-led method for AI-assisted course development used across UNSW College’s new Applied Degrees: industry co-designed, work-blended bachelor programs in business and information technology. It addresses two questions: how can generative AI support curriculum development at program scale while preserving human educational judgement; and where must that judgement be structurally embedded? The method is grounded in constructive alignment (Biggs & Tang, 2011) and human-centred AI (Le Dinh et al., 2025), applied at program rather than course level. The main focus is programmatic coherence. Rather than building courses one at a time, the method applies shared design patterns across an entire program. Even with different subject matter experts (SMEs) and program leads contributing to different courses, these design principles remain consistent from first year to capstone. AI generates content within this architecture, but functions as a structured design assistant rather than an autonomous author. Different workflow stages route to different AI models suited to each context. This preserves checkpoints where human framing and contextual judgement re-enter the process, consistent with calls to keep human control central to AI in education (Alfredo et al., 2024; Bearman et al., 2023; Hau, 2025; Islam, 2026). The human-led, AI-supported workflow moves from industry and academic SME input and course overview revision through curriculum blueprinting, assessment critique, rubric development, Canvas-ready asynchronous content, workshop planning, and student-facing resources. The assessment-critique stage is especially significant as generative AI reshapes what assessment must do, with recent scoping evidence showing AI is driving a re-examination of assessment design across student, teacher and institutional levels (Chiu et al., 2024). Human judgement remains decisive throughout: SMEs establish disciplinary intent; program leads review coherence and progression; learning designers evaluate scaffolding, accessibility and learner experience; and final quality assurance confirms alignment before publication. The ASCILITE Technology Enhanced Learning Accreditation Standards (TELAS, 2022) informed the design from the outset and now provide the basis for review, making quality auditable. This matters for Applied Degrees, where quality depends on integrating academic standards, industry relevance, work-integrated learning and inclusive learning design. Outputs are structured for continuous improvement in Canvas, keeping pedagogical authority close to the point of delivery rather than locked inside opaque AI outputs (UNESCO, 2023). Critically, automating the repetitive build frees human effort for the work most often skipped under time pressure: the programmatic view, gathering student feedback, time with industry to collect current case studies and simulations, and targeted employability development so graduates are work ready. AI can accelerate curriculum production while strengthening human-centred design, provided the architecture and its checkpoints are designed first. The contribution is that architecture. The design patterns, curriculum blueprinting and checkpoints where human judgement re-enters are transferable to other program-scale builds regardless of which AI tools are used.

Parsons problems have been widely recognised to support novice learners by reducing the cognitive demands of writing code from scratch through rearrangement of provided code blocks. A common variation includes distractors – erroneous blocks of code which do not belong to the correct solution. While Parsons problems have been widely studied for introductory programming, they remain underexplored in various domains including in data science education, where students may possess statistical knowledge but limited programming experience. Developing distractors is also time-consuming for educators. This study investigated the feasibility of using a large language model (LLM) to generate semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems. A set of distractors was generated for 315 Python-based data science Parsons problems and was evaluated for pedagogical plausibility, compilability, and output divergence. Validated distractors were then incorporated as exemplars in a refined prompt to generate a second set of distractors, which were evaluated using the same criteria. The findings demonstrate that LLMs can be used to develop semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems and refining the prompts using validated exemplars further improved the quality. This study contributes to the limited literature on data science Parsons problems, distractor design and LLM-supported development of these problems.
